Information Matrices

Source: R/information.R
information_objects.Rd

The information of a likelihood is the matrix of second derivatives that measures how sharply the log-likelihood \(\ell(\eta)\) peaks at the estimate \(\hat\eta\) of the parameters on the link scale. Its inverse is the estimated variance matrix of the estimates, so the choice of the matrix is the choice of the standard errors. Two objects select it, observed_info() and expected_info(), and both inherit from Information. A function that takes such an object, such as the vcov() method of a fit (see vcov.distrib_fit()), is told the matrix by the object and not by a character string. The argument information of those functions is NULL by default, which selects the matrix described under "The default" below.

Value

No value. The topic describes the two objects, of classes ObservedInfo and ExpectedInfo, that observed_info() and expected_info() return.

Details

observed_info()

The negative Hessian of the log-likelihood at the data, $$-\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial\eta\,\partial\eta^\top}\bigg|_{\hat\eta}.$$ It is computed from the second derivatives that the family supplies in closed form, or from their numerical fallbacks when the family supplies only a density. It takes no argument. It is the curvature of the likelihood in the sample at hand, and every family has it. It describes the uncertainty only where the log-likelihood is twice differentiable in every parameter at the estimate.

expected_info()

The Fisher information, $$\mathbb{E}\left[-\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial\eta\,\partial\eta^\top} \right]_{\hat\eta},$$ the average of the observed information over samples drawn from the model at the estimates. With method = NULL, the default, the closed form of the family is used where the family writes the expectation out (see expected_hessian_exact()), and expect_opg() otherwise. An object in method is used for every family, one of expect_opg(), expect_integrate() and expect_mc(); expected_derivative_methods compares the three.

The two matrices agree asymptotically and differ in a finite sample. The expected information is a function of the parameters alone and is positive definite wherever the family is regular. The observed information depends on the data, and it can be indefinite away from the estimate or at an outlier. Standard errors from the observed information describe the likelihood that was actually observed, which is the usual recommendation (Efron and Hinkley, 1978). For a family that has no closed-form expected information, expect_opg() is a noisier estimate of the information than the observed matrix.

The default

The argument information of vcov.distrib_fit(), confint.distrib_fit(), print.distrib_fit() and mv_summary() is NULL. It resolves to observed_info() when every parameter of the family has params_order() of at least 2, that is, when the log-likelihood is twice differentiable in every parameter, and to expected_info() with method = NULL otherwise, for the whole matrix. A family with a kink in a parameter (the Laplace, the elastic net) has a singular or undefined observed information in that parameter, and the closed-form expected information gives finite standard errors. A fit states which information it used whenever it is not the observed one.

References

Efron, B. and Hinkley, D. V. (1978). Assessing the accuracy of the maximum likelihood estimator: observed versus expected Fisher information. Biometrika, 65, 457-483.

See also

observed_info() and expected_info() for the constructors; Information for the classes; vcov.distrib_fit(), confint.distrib_fit() and mv_summary() for the functions that take the object; expected_derivative_methods for the methods of the expected information.

Examples

observed_info()
#> Observed information
expected_info()
#> Expected information (closed form where the family has one, otherwise the outer product of the scores)
expected_info(method = expect_integrate(identity = "score"))
#> Expected information (expectation by integration against the density (identity = score))

# The standard errors of one fit under the two matrices.
set.seed(1)
d <- gaussian1_distrib()
fit <- fit_distrib(d, distrib_rng(d, 300, list(mu = 1, sigma = 2)))
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, information = observed_info())))
#>         mu      sigma 
#> 0.11109240 0.07855419 
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, information = expected_info())))
#>         mu      sigma 
#> 0.11109240 0.07855419
